Stocks making the biggest moves midday: Nvidia, Moderna, IonQ, Airbnb, Firefly Aerospace & more
headlines.summary: Here are some of the companies making headlines in midday trading.
headlines.article_text: Stocks making the biggest moves midday: NVDA, MRNA, IONQ, ABNB, FLY Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Here are some of the companies making headlines in midday trading. IonQ – The quantum computing stock rose 17% after IonQ lifted its full-year guidance for revenue. The company sees revenue in a range of $505 million to $515 million, topping analysts' estimate for $456.2 million, per FactSet. Firefly Aerospace – The company announced a roughly $1.3 billion agreement with AST SpaceMobile in which it will provide 36 rocket engines and a license to the engine's intellectual property. Firefly surged nearly 30%, while AST SpaceMobile advanced 6%. Microchip Technology – The semiconductor manufacturer tumbled 14% on the back of largely disappointing guidance for the current quarter. Microchip Technology sees third-quarter non-GAAP earnings ranging from 87 cents to 95 cents per share and revenue between $1.573 billion to $1.638 billion. The FactSet consensus estimate called for 94 cents a share and $1.63 billion. Moderna — The vaccine maker rallied 7%. The company smashed third-quarter earnings estimates and raised its outlook for full-year sales growth. Moderna now expects 2026 revenue growth of 15% to 25%, up from previous guidance of no more than 10%. Lam Research — The semiconductor equipment maker surged nearly 9% after the board authorized a $25 billion stock buyback . Five9 — The cloud-based contact-center-as-a-service provider fell more than 17%. Five9 lowered full-year adjusted EPS guidance and announced a $325 million cash acquisition of Level AI. Axon Enterprise — The Taser maker dropped 18% after third-quarter EPS and revenue missed Wall Street estimates, fourth-quarter guidance was weak and it pledged an additional $1.2 billion investment in drone maker Skydio, raising its stake to about 37%. Artificial intelligence and semiconductor stocks — Micron Technology, Sandisk , Marvell Technology, Advanced Micro Devices , Nebius and CoreWeave climbed Friday, recovering ground after Thursday's sharp sell-off amid concerns over potential constraints on AI data-center expansion. Nvidia rebounded more than 3% and returned to positive territory for 2026. Cloudflare — Shares climbed about 12% after guidance for the current quarter topped Street expectations. Cloudflare forecast adjusted earnings of 43 cents a share versus the LSEG consensus for 38 cents, on revenue of $845 million to $846 million, higher than analysts' consensus of $798 million. Iren – The neocloud provider jumped 19% after fiscal first-quarter revenue of $228 million grew from $137 million the prior quarter. More than $4 billion in annual recurring revenue projected to arrive in 2026 has been delayed until at least January 2027. Iren has been battered in the latest rout of AI-focused stocks, dropping 31% in the past week. Airbnb — The online lodging marketplace jumped 11% after third-quarter earnings of $3.16 per share topped analysts' consensus estimate of $2.85. Revenue of $4.87 billion beat the Street's $4.75 billion estimate, LSEG data showed. Atlassian — Shares dropped more than 14% after the supplier of team collaboration and productivity software showed year-over-year data center revenue growth expected to decline approximately 14% in the fiscal second quarter ending in December, and 16% in the fiscal year ending next June. JFrog — The software company soared 35% after raising full-year guidance. JFrog sees adjusted earnings ranging from $1.14 to $1.16 per share on revenue of $680 million to $682 million. The outlook trounced FactSet consensus estimates of 98 cents a share and $651.9 million. DraftKings — The online sports betting platform tumbled 27%. DraftKings posted a wider-than-expected third-quarter loss of 94 cents per share, worse than the 39 cent loss analysts polled by LSEG anticipated. Revenue of $1.33 billion fell short of the $1.40 billion estimate. Sportsbook revenue totaled $784 million, missing the $811.8 million StreetAccount consensus estimate. Lyft — The ridesharing company fell almost 5%. Third-quarter revenue of $1.82 billion trailed the FactSet consensus among analysts for $1.92 billion, while fourth-quarter guidance for bookings came in at $5.74 billion to $5.94 billion versus the FactSet consensus of $5.81 billion. — CNBC's Nick Wells, Darla Mercado and Scott Schnipper contributed reporting

headlines.title: The AI ‘credit card’ is getting costlier as CoreWeave bond yield tops 16%
headlines.summary: Coreweave's steep yields reflect stress in the AI debt markets as investors worry about a data center slowdown. What comes next.
headlines.article_text: CoreWeave bond yield tops 16% as AI credit stress rises Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points CoreWeave’s bond yield has climbed above 16%, highlighting investor concern about financing the AI infrastructure boom. Default protection costs have risen across AI-linked companies, including Nvidia, Broadcom and Oracle. Wall Street expects substantial borrowing to fund further AI expansion, making financing costs a key test for the spending boom. In this article ORCL GSBD Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Jonathan Raa | Nurphoto | Getty Images Debt markets are sending a message to AI data center builders: we're hiking the interest rate on your credit card and may put some new curbs on your credit limit. That analogy comes courtesy of Jefferies global head of equity strategy, Christopher Wood, who put it in a note on Friday: "The most plausible way the AI capex arms race will end is that the credit card will be taken away." That isn't happening yet, but credit markets have been spooked by the new political landscape — seeing more hurdles to data centers under Democratic governors in key states, along with a Democratic-controlled Congress. The poster child for debt stress is neocloud Coreweave . The yield on its 2032 bond with a 9.625% coupon has climbed above 16%. Coreweave's five-year credit default swaps spiked above 1,289 basis points on Thursday, widening above their October peak, according to Deutsche Bank. The CDS eased 8% Friday to around 1,155. "We've had plenty of warnings from the credit space," said Jim Reid, Deutsche Bank's global head of macro and thematic research, in a note on Friday. Debt and equities are now moving more in sync, he added, "so we'll have to see if credit goes any further." Investors are demanding more compensation to insure against default among even companies with the strongest balance sheets and credit ratings, including Nvidia , Broadcom , and Amazon.com . CDS on Nvidia debt is up 76% in the last month. Broadcom's CDS is up 49%, while Amazon's has gained 44%. Their CDS remain low on an absolute basis; Nvidia's spread stood at roughly 139 basis points, compared with about 298 bps for Oracle and roughly 1,100 for CoreWeave. A large increase from a low starting point does not imply the same credit risk. Still, rising CDS are a sign that markets want more protection against default among even the largest and healthiest debt issuers. And rising CDS imply higher financing costs down the line. The market is now grappling with the prospect that at least some data center spending will be delayed or scrapped under incoming Democratic governors in Ohio, Texas, and Georgia, the three states with much of the planned capacity. Moratoriums could impact 45% of planned capacity in the U.S. with a large amount of that in Texas, according to Goldman Sachs. Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has said she's not opposed to data centers but wants a moratorium until the state legislature passes protections for communities. None of these means AI debt financing is collapsing. Goldman tallies five AI bond deals totaling $67 billion since October 29, pushing total hyperscaler debt issuance this year to $296 billion. Goldman forecasts $440 billion of hyperscaler debt issuance next year, plus an additional $300 billion of project-level issuance across investment-grade and high-yield. The Trump administration is vowing to support data centers. National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett told CNBC on Friday that he expects data center growth to continue as forecast, despite Democrats' big election wins. What comes next The big question now is how quickly AI spending will generate enough cash for hyperscalers to keep investors comfortable with future capex plans. For the neoclouds, any sign of consolidation or retrenchment in capex could result in fewer or shorter contracts for data center compute or delays in prepayments. Goldman analysts said hyperscalers collectively reported negative free cash flow in the third quarter as capital spending exceeded operating cash flow. "Delayed monetization and growth in purchase commitments—which we view as additional and sizable uses of cash, separate from Capex—are the key risks to more debt issuance, subject to market conditions," according to the bank. Peak AI debt issuance may now be closer at hand. Bank of America analysts estimates that AI-related credit issuance will rise 31% from 2026 to 2027, hitting $685 billion, including public and private debt. They then see it falling 23% to $531 billion in 2028. As for the risk?
